utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Good morning, ladies and gentlemen. I am pleased to be here after a short Easter break. It is a little refreshing. May we have the appearances, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours. My name is Niemann and I appear with my colleagues, Ms. McHenry, Mr. Turone and Ms. Udo for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Could we have appearances for the Defence, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours. My name is Edina Residovic, Defence counsel for Mr. Zejnil Delalic, along with my colleague, Eugene O'Sullivan, professor from Canada

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours. My name is Zeljko Olujic, Defence attorney from Croatia, appearing on behalf of Mr. Zdravko Mucic, along with my colleague, Mr. Michael Greaves from the United Kingdom.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours. I am Salih Karabdic, attorney from Sarajevo, appearing on behalf of Mr. Hazim Delic, along with Mr. Thomas Moran, attorney from Houston, Texas.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours. I am Cynthia McMurrey and I represent Esad Landzo, along with Ms. Nancy Boler, from the United States

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I be allowed to address the court before the witness is brought into the courtroom?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: May we know the subject matter of such an address, because cross-examination is still continuing?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, your Honours, it is linked to that and to a number of errors that have occurred during the cross-examination, in connection with which I should like to give my explanations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Please, let us have the cross-examination continue. If you have any objection as to any particular cross-examination, you can raise that. You do not have to make addresses in between the activities of the cross-examination, which may not in any event be related. So, let us have the witness. If you have any reasons why you should object to cross-examination, we will hear that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honours. I will ask for your indulgence later on. (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Remind the witness he is still under oath.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I remind you, Sir, that you are still under oath.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understand. MUHAMED VEJZAGIC (continued)

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Brigadier, on the last occasion when we were -- when I was asking you some questions, I asked that you be shown a document marked 193. Perhaps that might be given to the Brigadier again. I believe I have some additional copies of that for your Honours (Handed). Brigadier, this document marked number 193, have you ever seen this before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you notice at the top of the document there is a reference to a number and then a date in the first paragraph. Do you see the number and date that appears there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you know what those numbers and dates relate to, by any chance?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The number I do not know and the date refers to the date the document was issued.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The date of the document with the number, yes, I see, but it does not relate to this particular document? I think I may have confused you. Let me try and clarify it for you. I am not talking about the number and date that appears on this particular document; I am talking about the number and date that appears in the body of the document in the first paragraph, where it says, "Pursuant to the appointment of the main command of the armed forces of BiH number" and then "of 11/07/1992" -- it is the BiH number 02/349-343 11/7/1992, that is the document. I am asking you, do you know what that relates to -- if you do not, it does not matter -- the date?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The date given is 11 July 1992, linked to the document, that is the date when that document was issued.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: My question is, do you know what that document is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The document mentioned here is the staff of the supreme command of 11 July when Mr. Delalic was appointed commander of Tactical Group 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you, yes. Now, would you look at this document that I show you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: May I just make an additional explanation? This refers to Tactical Group 1, Konjic. In the order issued on 11 July, there is no reference to Tactical Group 1, Konjic, but only to Tactical Group 1, so here we see something new. When we talk about appointments to various functions, there are too many here for a Tactical Group, that is one point I would like to make. We have the orders of the supreme command with reference to the Operation Jug, "South"; there are far fewer people even though the operation is more complicated and the command itself is more complex. Here, I do not see the person who was chief of staff at the time, so I do not see the chief of staff who was the chief of staff from the very first day the TG1 was formed, so I do not see that name here.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you for those observations. The next document I wanted you to look at -- that should be given the next number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution document number 230.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Again, this document of 1 August 1992, have you seen this one before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is an appointment for administrative affairs, office work. I think I do have such a document as far as I can recall -- I am not quite sure, but I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You believe that you have seen it before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: It was not included among your material, but it is a document that you consider to be a valid document, do you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot assert as a handwriting expert, because I am not an expert for handwriting, whether this is Mr. Delalic's signature or not. I just see the appointment for a Ms.. Nermina Bukvic or something like that -- the copy is a bad one, so I cannot quite read it -- Habiba Bukvic, I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: It has the stamp and other indicia of reliability attached to it, does it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, you cannot see the stamp -- it is black ink and you cannot tell what type of stamp was used.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Might that be marked for identification, if your Honours please? Brigadier, when was Mr. Delalic appointed commander of Tactical Group 1?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On 11 July 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: We have seen in your documents, and you do not need to go to them unless you want to, but in your documents marked 64 and 65, the two appointments of Mr. Delalic, respectively of 11 July 1992 and 27 July 1992, both signed by Sefer Halilovic, you would agree with me that both documents are valid, would you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And you would agree with me that the commander of Celebici complex, when it was run as a prison, was part of the Bosnian army and thus under the authority of the supreme command?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You did not mention a name -- I do not know who you are referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Perhaps you might tell us that. Who do you consider was the commander of Celebici camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: According to the research I did, I would not call it a "camp" -- it was a prison formed out of necessity, because of the large number of captives and who was responsible for that prison, I cannot assert with certainty, because I did not find a single document whereby one would establish who was responsible for the prison -- because of the complexity of the situation and the war operations, one could see that both the HVO police and the MUP police were at first responsible for the prison. Who was the commander, I do not know -- I cannot assert that, because there is no document to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Just looking at D/42, if you would, for a moment, for me, please? Might I see the exhibit before it is shown to the witness -- I just want to check that I have the right one. I am sorry, it is V-D/42 -- it is in the binders and it is in the third binder. It could be left in the binder -- just pass the binder. For your Honours benefit, it is page 819. (Handed). Brigadier, this is one of the documents that you included in your papers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And the order is directed, is it not, to the commander of the prison?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The governor or warden or manager of the prison, not commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I do not know what the word you have in your version of it is, but mine says "commander" -- "commanding officer". Does yours not say "commanding officer"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I am sorry, let me explain. The commanders and commanding officers are people in charge of units, that is one concept. Another one are the managers or governors of institutions or chiefs of institutions who have no right of command, but right of management and, in my text, it says "to the manager of the prison" or "the warden".

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When I asked you who was "commander", you have answered it literally according to your interpretation. Let us start again. Who was manager of the prison based on your interpretation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: According to this, we see that the manager of the prison at the time was Mr. Zdravko Mucic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You do not doubt the validity of this document, do you -- you are not suggesting it is not a valid document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I do not doubt it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You would agree with me that this document says -- it is issued on the basis of the order of the supreme command, so that the supreme command headquarters in Sarajevo would have authority over the prison complex at Celebici, would it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What is the meaning of the word on the basis of the order issued at the very beginning of the order?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What this is is that the supreme command issued this order to the commander of the Tactical Group and it is not the prison that is under the supreme command. Therefore, the supreme command gives orders to the commander of the Tactical Group, who is subordinated to him, to deal with the problem in connection with the prison. In this case, it has to do with the formation of a commission for the interrogation of prisoners. Therefore, the supreme command issues orders to the commander of the Tactical Group and not to the manager of the Celebici prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Are you suggesting that the supreme command has no authority over the prison -- is that what you are saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: In relation to the document that you are now looking at and other documents that you have seen, we have the order numbers of the documents typed immediately above the date in most instances. You said last Thursday that you could not tell us what those numbers signify. Am I correct in assuming that, at least in 1992, you yourself did not issue any written orders?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know what you are referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I am simply asking you a question. Did you issue orders yourself -- written orders -- in 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was not authorised to issue any orders. Orders are only issued by the commander and I did not hold the post of commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You worked for the supreme command, but when you were working for the supreme command, you issued no orders -- that is my point?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I worked on the drafting of orders. It is one thing to prepare an order and it is another to issue an order. No other person has the authority to issue orders, save the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I am right in assuming, am I not, that the supreme command had authority over the municipal headquarters of the Tactical Defence -- sorry, the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This means the Territorial Defence staff of Konjic and Jablanica who were not within the district staff of Mostar, which at that time was still not functional. All the other municipal staffs were subordinated to district staffs, so there was this chain of authority. The municipal staffs were subordinated to district staffs and the district staffs were subordinated to the supreme command staff. In this case, this was a specific case in Konjic and Jablanica. The district staff in Mostar -- had that district staff in Mostar been functional, they would not have been directly subordinated to the supreme command in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: But in fact, they were, in 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they were. The municipal staff of Konjic and Jablanica were directly subordinated to the supreme command, because there was no other intermediate level.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: So that if the supreme command wanted to give a Tactical Group or an operative group authority over municipal headquarters of the Territorial Defence, then there is no question that it had the authority to do that, should it want to do so, in Konjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In this case, we are probably dealing with an order of the supreme command, which was probably not being implemented or it was not implemented on time. So, the supreme command, through the commander of the Tactical Group, is sending an urgent message that the problem should be tackled -- whether at the time there was a direct connection between the supreme command and the municipal command, I cannot say, and why the commander of the Tactical Group is being asked to deal with the problem, but, obviously, from the preamble of this document, it is evident that the signatory of this document is calling on this problem being resolved as soon as possible. So, it is not the commander of the Tactical Group who is involved here, but the --

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Nobody asked you that, and you did not answer my question. I really would appreciate it if you would just answer my question. My question has nothing to do with that document -- it is a general question. My question is this: did the supreme commander in Sarajevo have authority over the municipal headquarters of the Territorial Defence? It is a simple "Yes" or "No" answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The witness has several times, in the examination-in-chief and the cross-examination, answered this question with precision already.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Perhaps I might be directed to it in the transcript, if that is the case, because I have not seen it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: See the organisational chart which is prepared and he has made the -- he has shown the municipal staff to be directly under the supreme headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: That is a document that we object to most strenuously, because the witness that prepared it is not here to testify. We have no idea --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: But that is his position.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I will move on. You said in your evidence a report from an investigating commission is normally the kind of report that can be relied upon. I note from your documents that, in addition to such reports, you have included some verdicts from military courts. So, I presume you will agree with me that decisions of military courts are also the kinds of documents that normally can be relied upon; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Those are verdicts from 1995, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: It does not matter when they are. I am just asking, are they the sort of documents that normally can be relied upon?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Probably, yes. I did not study that problem. I did not go into legal issues or the work of the judiciary. I did not consider that to be my duty. I am a military expert.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You saw fit to put them in your documents so presumably they serve some purpose?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Their purpose is to show that, with the formation of courts, justice started to function and criminals were brought to justice. That is the only reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Might the witness be shown the document marked Prosecution Exhibit 139, please? I have some additional copies for your Honours. (Handed). Brigadier, have you seen this document before? Has it ever been shown to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Is it a document that you took into account when you prepared your report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: May I have a look at it first, please? (Pause) I am sorry, I had not seen this one. I thought it was another document on a trial -- this one I have not seen.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honours, may we object to this? Number 1, of course, the witness has said that he has never seen it, he did not rely upon it in preparing his report and it is just an attempt by the Prosecution to introduce to the court evidence that has already been ruled inadmissible and irrelevant to these proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: I join that objection. As I recall, when this document was admitted, it was admitted for a sole purpose --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: It relates to the previous conviction of two of the accused before us.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I am not introducing it for that purpose. I want to know whether he relied on it for his report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Why are you referring to this document -- to show what?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Whether he relied on it, because it makes reference to the role of Mr. Delalic in the document. I wondered whether he considered it when he prepared his report -- if he has not seen it, he obviously did not consider it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I do not think he even saw it. You need not continue with this.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: May I ask that the documents be taken back from the court, since they are not introduced into evidence at this point for any purpose whatsoever?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I am marking them for identification. She can raise her objections --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: He cannot identify what he has not even seen.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I am not asking him to identify it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: He could not -- why should he identify it?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I am not asking it be identified. I asked that it be marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I do not think so -- I do not think it is necessary. It will not be so marked.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: It has already been marked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: It will not be -- the trial deputy should not so mark it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You said in your evidence that Serb villagers in the Konjic municipality did not abide by international rules of war. What international rules of war did they violate?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness's microphone is not switched on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The question is not precise. Will you please repeat it in a precise form?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes. You said in your evidence, page 10625, that the Serb forces in the villages of Konjic did not abide by international rules of war. I am simply asking you what rules of war the Serb villagers in the Konjic municipality did not abide by?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not speak about that during my testimony, or I do not recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You were asked the question on page 10625 by

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: "No, no, no, before those who were armed, those who were hiding, those who were undertaking certain operations against the State, were they abiding by international military law?" I think Mr. Moran may have asked this question. You said "no". Do you remember being asked that question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: We will not pursue it. So far as you know, the Serb forces in the villages of Konjic did abide by international law -- you would not know one way or the other.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You did not ask that question, did you?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: He said in his evidence that they did not. He now says he does not remember the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: It is now the opposite.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: He cannot say one way or the other.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You put that question to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You cannot say one way or the other whether they complied with international rules of war or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were considered rebels -- people rebelling against the constitution and working to overthrow the State -- whether they abided by the rules of warfare, I did not go into that problem. I do not remember having been asked that, whether they abided by those rules. I do not remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: There is evidence of a shelling on civilian population of Konjic from Borci.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is a problem with the Serbs -- the Serbs who organised defence before the beginning of the war. It is well known that they armed, that they captured positions around Konjic, and they destroyed the innocent population. Whether that is allowed by international military law, I do not know, because I am not a lawyer, but it is well known what they did. It is up to lawyers to say whether they abided by international law, when they killed children and citizens, if that is what you are referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The shelling of Borci was done by the JNA, was it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not just the JNA. It was the JNA that had armed them and they joined -- the rebel Serbs joined the JNA, the JNA itself could not have done it. They armed them and they operated together in Konjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: In 1992, when did the Bosnian army consider that a person was entitled to prisoner of war status and what was the procedure used to determine whether a person was entitled to that status.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: I am going to object to the first part of that compound question, because prisoner of war status is a question of law, not a question that is within the competence of this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The issue of what the Bosnian army took into account, when it determined whether a person was entitled to prisoner of war status, is a matter of fact. These are factual issues -- whether or not that in the end amounts to prisoner of war status under the Geneva Conventions is a question of law. I am not asking the witness that. The factual question as to what the army did and what it considered to be a person who was a prisoner of war is a perfectly appropriate question, based on fact. The witness comes here to the court, he holds himself out as an expert in military matters, he holds himself out as an expert on the Bosnian army and I think he is perfectly entitled to answer the question. He may not know the answer to the question, but, if it is within his area of competence -- and one presumes it is -- then it is an appropriate question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would suggest that the Judge Advocate General of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina would be the appropriate person to answer that question, not a staff officer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I do not think you need argue that. Can the witness attempt an answer? If he does not know, he can say so. When do you consider a person to have prisoner of war status -- it is simple.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My personal conviction is if he was armed and if he was on the opposing side and captured as such, he is a prisoner of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You have testified about problems with the siege of Sarajevo and the problems that created for the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. You would agree with me, would you not, that the lifting of the siege was a goal of the Bosnian army well past the end of 1992 -- it did not finish somewhere in the middle of 1992, but it went well beyond that, did it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: It did not go past the middle of 1992 -- that was the end of the problem?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The problem of the siege of Sarajevo did not end in the middle of 1992. The problem of the siege of the city continued.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And well past 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Are you expecting me to answer? I do not understand -- yes, the problem continued. The blockade was not lifted until the withdrawal of the Serb forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you were going through some of your documents, you said in respect of some of them that you were convinced that those documents existed in archives, and those were the words that you used, that you were convinced they existed in archives. When you said that, were you stating that you actually saw them in archives, or were you just stating an opinion that you were convinced that they were there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: While working on my expert report, I have 42 documents listed that I found, but I have not seen everything, nor can I claim that everything exists, because the supreme command headquarters was shelled frequently, the location was changed, the supreme command headquarters is a large institution. Imagine how many documents. There were 12 departments apart from the supreme command and the operational centre, so I did not claim that I had seen everything, but according to my expert analysis I have 42 documents that were studied and listed in my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: That is all I am talking about. Were those documents seen by you in archives and taken from archives, or were they given to you by some other source, that is my only question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A part of the documents were obtained from the archives and a part were given to me by the defence, a part from the Institute for the Investigation of War Crimes. There were several sources, therefore.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you look at documents in the archives of the 443rd Brigade, which I believe is now in Konjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not have any such document.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you look at any army archives that had held in Konjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The documents issued by the staff or the joint command, those I have enclosed and I do not have any document from the 443rd Brigade. I have documents from the Croatian brigade of Herceg-Stjepan and that, too, has been enclosed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The person in charge of military archives in Konjic, did you speak to that person?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know which person was in charge of the archives -- I talked to the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What was his name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He is now the commander of the development group -- it is in the documents -- I cannot recall the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You cannot remember his name, thank you. Also in your evidence you spoke of the fact -- about the creation of war presidencies, and you spoke about it under the old law and under the new law. Under the old law, a war presidency could be established if there was an immediate threat of war, whereas under the new law the war presidency could only be created in periods of war; do you remember saying that, or to that effect in your evidence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In both cases, in both the old and new law, in fact, it was adopted from the old law. As soon as such a situation exists when the assembly cannot sit, the war presidency is established.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I see. So, you may not have said it, but you would disagree with me if I put to you that, under the new law, you could only create a war presidency if you were in a state of war, as opposed to an immediate threat of war -- you would disagree with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The war presidency is established whenever there are no conditions for the assembly to sit, that is, in circumstances of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I asked you last week when you were giving evidence if you could give me the names of any of the persons or persons that you had spoken to -- sorry, that you had spoken to and relied upon when compiling your report. Did you remember the name -- did you do that for me and remember the names of any of the persons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am a bit advanced in age, so my memory of names is a bit spotty, so, please, if you can avoid asking me those things as well as numbers. What I am really looking to do is look at the documents and I have really discussed matters with a whole range of people.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I asked you also whether you could tell me where you got the document from, dated 11 July 1992, appointing Mr. Delalic, where we had demonstrated that the word INDA-BAU had been removed. You were going to find out and tell me where you had got that from. Did you make any enquires about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I checked on that, and I was given this document by the defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And, finally, just a moment ago we were discussing about the authority of the supreme command over the municipal headquarters and I had asked you the question, did the supreme command have authority over the municipal headquarters? I do not think that we got an answer to that, because you then started to speak about TG1. I just ask you to look at this document that is now shown to you and it might be given the next number in order. (Handed).

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution document 231.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did review the document, so, please, you can ask your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Have you seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You worked with Sefer Halilovic, did you not, in the supreme command?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Are you familiar with his signature?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am familiar with the signature, but I cannot say that this is his signature, because a signature can always be counterfeited in certain ways. I am not saying that this is the case here.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Does it look like a counterfeit of Sefer's signature?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The stamp that appears on the document appears to be the regular and ordinary stamp that one would expect to find on a document of this kind?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Just in relation to the document, you would agree with me, would you not, that this indicates that the supreme command has authority to place the municipal headquarters under the immediate authority of an operational group or an operative group?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I object as to the relevance of this document. This is a completely different area of Vares and Visoko. It has nothing to do with the area that is relevant to this matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: It goes to authority. It is put to the witnesses as a basis of authority of the supreme command. If there is any suggestion -- if the Defence would be prepared to stipulate that the supreme command of the armed forces had the authority over the municipal headquarters and could place the municipal headquarters under the authority of an operative group, if they are prepared to stipulate to that, I will not proceed with the matter. If they are not prepared to stipulate to it, I think it is a fair question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: The witness can answer the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Could you answer the question, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have already stated what the system of subordination was. That is, the supreme command was at the top of the armed forces. Subordinated to them were the district staffs of the Territorial Defence and then, to them, the municipal staffs were subordinated, so this was the chain of command and here we are talking about the establishment of an operative group, so there is no direct subordination of the municipal staff to the supreme command -- to the staff of the supreme command. So, this jump can happen. For instance, here, the commander, by forming an operative group, is ordering -- that is, stating -- which units are going to be included there, but this is not the usual practice. So, the municipal staffs were usually subordinate to the district staffs. So, the supreme command staff did not necessarily need to communicate with the municipal staff, because he already had a subordinate intermediary staff that did that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Might the document be marked for identification, your Honours? Finally, Brigadier, do you remember whether one of the persons that you spoke to, when you compiled your report, was a person called Jasminka Dzumhur?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not get in touch with Ms. Dzumhur -- I do not know her. I thought it was not part of the military expertise area.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: That is all for the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have some questions, but, first, I would like to ask whether it would not be better if we were to resume at 12?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: It will not be better. You had better start your re-examination now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Before re-examination starts, I would like to know, what was the precise role of MUP in Konjic in 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Konjic MUP was subordinate to the Ministry of the Interior of the Bosnian State. Its role was to keep the public law and order and, in addition to the regular police forces, there were reserve police forces, which are mobilised in wartime. They assist the regular police forces, but they could also be used in combat operations. They were a component member of the armed forces. They had the right to arrest, to remand persons in custody, so they had all the regular duties that a civilian police force does and the reserve police force was also -- could also be used in combat operations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Ms.. Residovic, I thought you did not need any extra time to study the matter, because, in re-examination, you are limited to areas which are still ambiguous arising from cross-examination. I did not think there were so many areas of that type.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour, I will try to limit myself to exactly such questions. I did have sufficient time after the cross-examination of the Prosecutor, because we had a holiday recess, so I did prepare. I respect your decisions, and so I would like to also be directed in a manner that would not throw me off. Now, I would like to go back to the issue which I tried to raise before this witness came back this morning, because I believe as the Defence counsel I need to raise them with the Trial Chamber. In the evidence which was offered together with the expert report in part 3, V-D/53 in the Bosnian language on page 852 and, in English, at 854, there is a list of 32 names and in place 31 there is a name, Risto Vukalo which was erroneous. It was offered by the Prosecution as Exhibit 225 and Mr. Niemann talked about it on page 10950 of the transcript. This document does not contain, under 31, the name of Risto Vukalo. I would like to remind the Trial Chamber that the Defence identified the same document here under number D114/1 -- it is the identical document, and this document was provided at a much earlier stage to the Prosecution and in this document 114 there is not the name of Risto Vukalo -- it was brought in and identified by the witness Arif Sultanic. This document was provided by the Prosecution to the Defence. It was shown to the Trial Chamber. Even though this document was not accepted into evidence, it was offered to the Trial Chamber and the Defence also offered it to the Defence expert witness. Right now, I cannot go into details about all the difficulties we encounter in Sarajevo when we are trying to either have these documents copied and translated, but I would like to point out that this is simply a technical error and this is the first issue that I wanted to draw your attention to. The second issue that Mr. Niemann pointed out is the document that the witness showed at VI/4 and it is page 896 in Bosnian and 897 in English -- INDA-BAU does not appear in the Bosnian text -- it is in the English translation of the text that was enclosed together with the expert report of this witness. You know well that this document was admitted with the word "INDA-BAU" included and it was included as 997/9. If you will recall, it was the Defence which insisted that the name, the date and the fax number would be marked, because this is a document that my client himself identified when he was questioned by the Prosecution office. So, what I am going to say is that, again, this is a technical error. The witness received this document from the Defence, and I request that these explanations be accepted and there are English translations. Thirdly, the chart TG1 which was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You have sufficient time to make explanations. Can you re-examine the witness? If there is some question arising from cross-examination, which this witness has to give, you make your re-examination and he will make the explanation. It is not for you as counsel to say what he should say. I agree there are explanations which counsel can make, but if it is an explanation which the witness should himself give, ask your question so that he will be able to make the explanation himself. You should not keep him sitting there with you making explanations which he should make.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, these are issues raised by the Prosecutor in cross-examination and these are documents received by the witness from the Defence. Since these were errors in documents that the Defence provided, I thought that it was my duty before this Trial Chamber to point out those facts. If there is an error in the chart and if the Defence is able to call General Polutak, then we would be able to explain this correction. Let me tell you, if I did not raise these issues, I would not feel well as Defence counsel for my client.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: If you have any questions arising from cross-examination, kindly put them to the witness. He will make his explanations

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Brigadier, during the cross-examination by the Prosecutor, you reiterated your statement that the coordinator was not a military position. Can you -- and that it was a very specific type of a role. Can you tell me whether your experience and your expertise, based on your work within the armed forces, whether, on this basis you can give your opinion on when the coordinator -- the role of the coordinator arose during that period?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot hear the interpretation -- the English interpretation.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpretation was complete.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Kindly check his earphones.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Something is not working. Mr. Usher, can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The concept of coordinator does not refer exclusively to the military structures. To "coordinate" means to bring something into agreement, so there was a need to link things, to make them work together, both in civilian and military matters.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Can you now tell me, in 1992, how often would you encounter this role of a coordinator?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: There is no question about whether there was a coordinator or Tactical Group commander -- there is nothing.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The last question here: was this specific to Konjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it was not specific to Konjic. This happened throughout the country wherever there was that kind of problem, wherever there were multiple participants, somebody had to be inserted to work on solving these problems.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Brigadier, I am going to ask you a different kind of question now. You were shown an order which allegedly was signed by Mr. Delalic on 14 November. Can you please tell me, with your experience, when a certain problem was identified, what was the way in which the supreme command responded to it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were different problems which were of a similar nature. For instance, when we would go to visit the positions --

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Brigadier, if I can interrupt you, can you be more specific in your answer? If a certain wider problem was being identified, what was done in 1992 by the supreme command?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, if there was a problem of various commands of the various corps, what was done was a circular order would be issued to all commands, so this would be circulated around to all the respective commands.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: On page 10945 and further in the transcript, you said that this could have been a circular order. What prompted you to give this answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When reviewing this document, I saw that it was not characteristic for Konjic alone. It was a problem that, at the time, was present in the army and I did not know whether this was the intelligence department that said to circulate it around to all the reconnaissance units and the intelligence units.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 10918 you were asked a series of questions by the Prosecutor relating to the law on defence. Brigadier, can you now tell me whether any of the provisions of the law on defence puts the municipality in the position of command and control of the armed forces?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think I already responded to it unequivocally. I do not think there is a need for me to repeat. The presidency of the municipality has absolutely no authority over the armed forces units in terms of command and control.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Brigadier, in your research, did you find any document based on this law which was signed by the coordinator -- linked to the prisons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, there was only this document which was introduced a moment ago relating to the establishment of the commission which was to interrogate prisoners. That is the only one linked to the prisons.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Can you tell me how a subordinate soldier, when he addresses his superior, how did he address him in the former JNA, that is, with what title would he use?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the former Yugoslav People's Army, whose rules we adopted at the beginning of the war, when the superior calls him, he would address him, "Yes, Comrade Captain" and at that time there were no "Mr.", it was "Comrade" and then you would add the rank.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. After 1992, in our own army, when the Bosnia-Herzegovina became an independent State, how did --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I do not see how this arises out of the cross-examination. It has no place.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I am going to ask that this be allowed, because there are two relevant points that I would like to make -- a videotape was shown to the witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You are not being fair to the cross-examiner, who merely limited his questions to areas which, if there were any doubts, you were expected to re-examine. Limit yourself to those areas, instead of wandering off and dealing with areas which are not relevant to this examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Let me tell you the grounds. The film was shown to show Delalic as a person of authority -- of superior authority -- and we wish to show that the translation offered by the Prosecution puts Mr. Delalic in an ambiguous position. That is why I wanted to ask the witness and suggest that we view the tape once again to see the error made in the translation and in the position of Mr. Delalic as a person of superior authority.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You delight in wasting time -- if you do, you can continue. I think it has nothing to do with the cross-examination which I have listened to. There is no reference -- there is nothing ambiguous, Mr. Delalic himself was a superior of this group -- he was the commander of the TG1 and there is no question about that. Nobody has doubted that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, the tape referred to a period when Mr. Delalic was a coordinator --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Let us not continue with this argument. There is no need for it.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: May I be allowed to show the film that was shown by the Prosecutor to this witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I have indicated to you it has nothing to do with the cross-examination. But you are still insisting.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, we would like to offer a translation of this document as a correct translation, and we feel that this shows doubt as to the position of my client, raised through the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I have not listened to any question which raised any doubt whatsoever. Ask him any questions which you think arises from cross-examination. Those are the only things you should do. I think you are taking the indulgences too far.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I -- I may perhaps ask for a private session at one point, but now I should like to address the -- a question to the witness linked to the cross-examination. Brigadier, if a soldier addresses somebody without giving the title or rank, saying, "Mr." or "Mr. Commander", is he addressing his superior officer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In our army, at the beginning of the war when there were no ranks until November 1993, the subordinate would always address his superior, "Yes, Mr. Commander". When ranks were introduced, then he would say, "Yes, Mr. Commander", "Mr. General", "Mr. Colonel". So he would rank. If there were no ranks, then he would add the title.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Brigadier, if a soldier is not addressing the person with the words "Mr. Commander", or any other rank, does that mean that he is his superior?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If he did not use the term "Mr. Commander", or "Mr." with the rank, then that does not -- that means that he was not his superior.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, since the translation offered by the Prosecutor of his exhibit shown to this witness contained those very words, this was a reason for ambiguity and that is why we felt it necessary to clear this up. We would like to offer a correct translation of this dialogue so that the court may make its own conclusion as to its --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: What is ambiguous in the dialogue?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: -- as to the situation. A soldier addressing Delalic does not use the words given in the translation. He does not say, "Yes, Sir". In the text that we were given as a translation of this document, there is the word "Sir", both when addressing Padalovic and Captain Galanic. Therefore, the existence of this term is indicative of a superior position and that is the ambiguity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: The witness has explained it. He need not say anything further.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Brigadier, tell us whether you are familiar with the correspondence between the Konjic municipal staff, the Zenica staff and the supreme command regarding the relocation of the prison?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, in my report, there are two documents -- the municipal headquarters of Konjic addresses the supreme command with a request that the prisoners from Celebici be moved to Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Brigadier, did you check the validity of these documents in the army archives of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Brigadier, are you personally aware that a provisional command of the Group South was formed in which Zejnil Delalic was assistant commander for logistics?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you check this document in the archives of the Bosnian army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honours, I have no further questions of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I think this is all we have for this witness. Thank you very much, Brigadier, you have been very helpful. You have spent -- I am unable to count the number of hours you have spent sitting there answering questions intelligently and in the expert manner in which you have been put forward. We are very grateful for your assistance and for all your effort in explaining so many things which were still obscure to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Residovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, in view of the fact that, at the end of the examination-in-chief, as far as I was able to understand your ruling, you found that the expert report compiled by the expert is acceptable. I wish to tender it into evidence. At the same time, I am also tendering the documents contained in three volumes, appended to the report, to be admitted as the grounds on the basis of which this expert compiled his report and testified in court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I suppose it is admissible as evidence and the annexes as documents on which he based his opinion are admissible. You can tender them.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I am sorry, your Honours, I did not hear the translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: The report itself is an exhibit and the annexes are admitted as documents on which he based his opinion. They are admissible -- the report, distinct from the documents. The documents are not by themselves the truth of what they contain, but they are the basis on which he relied for his opinion. We accept it for that purpose. The difference is that you cannot single them out for purposes other than the fact that he based his opinion on them and the annexes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I understand your ruling. May I just ask that, in view of the fact that among the documents there are several drawings made by the witness himself, and we had a similar problem when it came to the admission of documents by Professor Hadzibegovic, does that mean the documents made by this expert personally can be admitted as evidence within the three volumes of other documents which are used as documents on which he relied upon for his opinions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: The annexes are admissible separately from the report itself. All documents he relied upon in the report itself are admissible for that purpose, but all those which are in the annexes which he did not by himself make or which he is not putting forward as having been made by himself are relied upon as documents on which he based his opinion.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I understand now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I think that is all. Thank you very much. The witness can now be discharged.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honours. (The witness withdrew)

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: May I ask the Registry to give us the numbers of the exhibits admitted? That is, the number for the report and the other documents in support of the opinions of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Before we interrupted the last witness, we were dealing with the Defence witness. Can we continue with him now?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: May Mr. Sultanic be called in. Will you please give us the number of the exhibit?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The report is number D143/1, and the annexes are D143A/1, D144/1 and 145/1. (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Please remind the witness he is still on his oath.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I remind you, Sir, that you are still under oath.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You may proceed, Ms.. Residovic. ARIF SULTANIC (continued)

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Sultanic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: To facilitate understanding of our conversation, I would like to ask you to wait for the translation that you can here on the headphones before answering my question. Mr. Sultanic, did you some time in 1992 meet Mr. Zejnil Delalic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Actually, on 2 June 1992, I met Mr. Zejnil Delalic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you know Mr. Zejnil Delalic from before, that is, prior to 2 June 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I was not acquainted with this gentleman, but I had heard of him, that as a relatively young man he had gone abroad to Germany and Austria and that he was in business.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I apologise. My client has just sent me a message asking if he may be allowed to be excused for a few minutes, because he has been here since 10 this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, he may be excused while you continue. We would not rise for that purpose -- he may be excused. The security guards can take him out.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Sultanic, why do you recollect that particular date, 2 June 1992, as being the date when you were introduced to Mr. Delalic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot hear anything on these earphones. I cannot hear any voice from the earphones, so I cannot check whether there has been any translation or not. Could you please repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sultanic, can you explain to this court why it is you remember that particular 2 June 1992 as being the day when you met Mr. Zejnil Delalic for the first time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I remember that date, because, after that meeting, we enabled the first train to run in exactly five days' time, so that the train started operating five days later on 7 June on the part of the railroad from Pazarici, and we were working on this around the clock for five days.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you tell us where it was that you met Mr. Delalic for the first time on 2 June?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On 2 June we met Mr. Delalic in front of his house and in the ground floor of his house.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Who was with you when you met with Mr. Delalic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was a group of railway workers -- Gorlic, Ramic and myself and somebody called Juzopovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Why did you go to see Mr. Zejnil Delalic on that day, 2 June -- who was it that sent you to him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Actually, as an organisation of public importance, that is, the railways were a public enterprise, and we had our own coordinating committee of experts whose task it was to mobilise transportation in this part of Bosnia-Herzegovina. We addressed ourselves to several institutions in the municipality, or, rather, the economic staff of the municipality, to consult them and to inform them about this issue, and since we had a lot of difficulty in obtaining some materials. We also did not have proper carriages, because this part of the railroad ran through a hilly area and we needed a vehicle as well as the gas for such a vehicle -- a heavy duty vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: What did they tell you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Excuse me. Leave that to the cross-examiner to give us those details -- how did he remember that date. You can leave these questions to the Prosecutor, to bring them out in cross-examination if he wants to know.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sultanic, what did they tell you in the economic staff?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The people in that staff told us to address ourselves to Mr. Zejnil Delalic, because he was assisting the economic staff as well as the army and its structures and the TO.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In the economic staff -- no, I am sorry, how did you understand the role of Zejnil Delalic after the economic staff members told you to contact him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We understood that he had been designated to carry out this task together with us.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: What was Zejnil Delalic's reaction to this idea of yours?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Having heard what we had to say and what we needed, he said that it was a good idea and in view of the difficulties with transportation and communication in general, because petrol and gas were in short supply, and rail transport is far less expensive and safer and better therefore, so he supported the idea and he said he would do his best to see, with the responsible people in the municipality, to get some kind of permits or certificates allowing us to move along the railway tracks and through various checkpoints held by the military police, the MUP. So we needed these certificates to be able to move around unhindered in carrying out our tasks.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did Mr. Delalic succeed in getting you these permits or permission for your work?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, already the next day Mr. Delalic brought something in the form of an order saying that it was his duty, together with the other people from the railways, to carry out this task, and at the same time he brought in these permits, like visiting cards, something like that, allowing us to move freely from Pazarici to Jablanica.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: May the witness now be shown Prosecutor's exhibit -- I apologise, I did not know how long the cross-examination would last, so I did not have the documents ready, but they are here now -- Exhibit 127? I have sufficient copies for the witness, for the court and for the Prosecutor. (Handed). Mr. Sultanic, will you please examine this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I remember this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sultanic, have you seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw it the day it was brought in by Mr. Zejnil Delalic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In your understanding of this document, and what you were doing, together with Mr. Zejnil Delalic, what was Mr. Delalic's role in the execution of this task?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: His role was to coordinate all these activities, together with us, and, upon the completion of the task, to report back to the municipal authorities and the TO command, that is, the joint staff of the TO and the HVO, which of course he did. Because he was working on this task with us, sometimes, maybe once or twice, his brother drove this car and obtained the reproduction material we needed, and the fuel.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Sultanic, could you please tell me whether, when you reached Mr. Delalic's house on the ground floor, did you see any officers or any soldiers that Mr. Delalic could have been in command of?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, there were no soldiers there. There was a kind of depot with some uniforms and some communications equipment, but there were no soldiers there.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sultanic, when you met Mr. Delalic and while you were working with him, did he have any military or civilian function?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, he did not have any military or civilian function. The only thing was that he was a coordinator between the military and the municipal body such as the railway, the post office, the distribution and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sultanic, could, at that time, Mr. Delalic give you any kind of orders?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, under no circumstances -- he could not have ordered us, because we were -- this was a job for railway men, and he could just assist us. He could not give us orders, nor did he try to give us orders, because he had no authority to give orders.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sultanic, in view of the fact that this project took five days, tell me, when did the train start operating on this part of the railway line?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The train became operational on 7 June, on a Sunday, 1992. I remember that day very well, because that morning about 100 refugees had come to Konjic on trucks, and we told them, because we saw them, in a kind of kindergarten -- I think it was a kindergarten -- we told them that the next people that come and others that will be leaving Konjic, even they, if they leave Konjic, would not have to go on trucks, open trucks, but they could use the train, as it was set into operation that day.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sultanic, was 7 June a peaceful day in Konjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, on the contrary. It was a very stormy day, because that very morning the sirens sounded the alarm for shelling, and just after the train had left towards Jablanica, the shelling of the city started.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I think we will rise now and reassemble at 2.30 p.m. (12.30 p.m.) (Luncheon adjournment) 17 18 19 20 21 22 23 24 25 (4.15 p.m.) (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You may proceed, Ms.. Residovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Kindly inform the witness he is still on his oath.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I remind you, Sir, that you are still under oath.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am aware of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sultanic, before the recess, we were looking at an order which was the basis of your working with Mr. Delalic on establishing the train runs. Mr. Sultanic, based on what Mr. Delalic was doing together with you, was he in a position where he could order you, or where he could adopt decisions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I also earlier stated that Mr. Delalic could not adopt any decisions or order us, so I think that that is nonsense.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that you remembered this day, because a lot of refugees arrived. Could you please tell me now, why do you recall the arrival of refugees on that day, or, to try to put it more precisely, where did these refugees come from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: These refugees came from Foca, that is eastern Bosnia. They came in large numbers, and so I remember that day when this train went and they said that they would not have to take cars or walk that part of the way.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sultanic, as far as you know, when did the refugees start arriving in large numbers in Konjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In late April and early May, they were coming in groups of up to 50 persons. They were going through the forests and through some mountain roads.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: What happened after Bradina -- after the blockade was lifted from Bradina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After the blockade of Bradina was lifted, everything went on the train from Pazarici, that is from the foothills of Igman to Jablanica where their ultimate destination was.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sultanic, can you tell me whether this celebration of starting the train runs was taped?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was filmed by several cameras.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Excuse me. Were you present at this manifestation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can the witness please be shown an excerpt -- a portion of the Prosecutor's Exhibit 116, which was the start of the train runs can we please have the tape played? It is the excerpt 3, which is the only one that I am going to offer. (Videotape played)

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: (Translating videotape). Maybe -- I would like to copy this timetable and forward it to the railway stations and other things. We have established the points for food, the numbers of persons and those who are responsible. The transport of refugees and travellers, disregarding their religion or nationality -- everything will be free. That is okay. I will go by car to warn them. Is it one or two? Let us do both -- there is no problem. Estimating the difficulties in regard to gasoline and difficulties in communication between citizens and the others who are now active, that is, our soldiers in this region between Jablanica and Pazarici, we found this communication would be established in the conditions that are prevalent now. We came here to Jablanica by train, we were very excited, the soldiers escorted us and we were who were there, the part of the reporter team came by car to wait for us here. The citizens of Jablanica know this is the first free train; not yet, as we have not yet given any public statement, but the citizens who need this will be informed very quickly, as soon as the first train comes. It means maybe even tomorrow, if it runs according to the timetable. Although you were not with us in the train, are you also excited about this train coming from Jablanica? Of course, as the one who was in charge of these project, I can say that I am satisfied. I also have to praise these people here, the railroad workers who took all this even more seriously.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Do you need this as part of your examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: This is the excerpt -- this excerpt takes about six or seven minutes and this is the Exhibit 116, which was accepted by the Trial Chamber, because of the relevance. Since we have a witness who was present at this event, this is the only opportunity that the Defence has to show what the role of Mr. Delalic was in this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Is there a difficulty with the role he played there? Nobody is disputing the role Delalic played there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: The train was known as the "Zejnil Express" -- we have some evidence to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, your Honours, but the entire 116 -- the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina is full of these irrelevant pieces of evidence about the role of Mr. Delalic, but the Trial Chamber did admit it into evidence as relevant for what his position was, so the witness here was present --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You assume a multiplication of irrelevant matters to anybody's case.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: No, we believe that it is irrelevant in the sense that he did not have any position of superiority, so we need to show what actually happened there.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Your Honour, please, microphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: The witness has already said he was just a coordinator -- he had no part in giving orders. He said that. Admittedly, he was a coordinator. What his functions were is part of the evidence. That is on the record. You have brought evidence what the coordinator's role was in the circumstances that Konjic was situated at that relevant time; how does it help us further?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: (INAUDIBLE).

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, your Honour, your microphone was not on, so I could not get the interpretation of what you just said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: All I said was that I do not think it will help us by competing in introducing irrelevant evidence. If one party is to introduce any irrelevant evidence, there is no point the Defence doing the same. It does not help the Trial Chamber at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Defence would like to be of assistance to the Trial Chamber in the best way it can, but let me repeat maybe what I have said several times. My client is charged with being coordinating -- with coordinating the military units since late May. If we do not show what we can, how can we prove that? You have already admitted this tape into evidence as relevant, in which case I do not understand what the Defence is, or whether the Defence is treated differently when it is trying to introduce its evidence. That is not my understanding now, because I was always under the impression that the Trial Chamber has been treating us equitably.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Go on.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Sultanic, do you also appear on this tape showing the start of the train run?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I am also in this videotape that shows the first train run.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you also give an interview to a journalist at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did give an interview to Vesna Bektasevic, who was a journalist for Radio Konjic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sultanic, what did you say your position was at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I told her that I felt very happy at that time, because we were able to start this island railroad. By that I meant that it was running in the area that was free and my particular function at that time was to oversee the electrical facilities, since the person who was in charge of that had left towards the end of April.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what was the name of this body in which you worked at the railroads?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This body was called the crisis staff of railroad workers. We took over the regulations of the Yugoslav railways and according to these rules, which we adopted, the traffic of trains was regulated for both peacetime and wartime and so we were in this body.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Will you please allow me to ask some further questions now? So, on this date, on 7 June 1992, was there a similar body in the municipality; in other words, was there a crisis staff in the municipality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no -- there was an economic staff in the municipality. There was no crisis staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sultanic, with whom in this crisis staff at your company did you work -- that you cooperated with in the municipal authorities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We worked together with the economic staff and I think that it was either Mr. Rebic or Mr. Dzejic who was in charge of the economic staff. He told us to turn to Mr. Zejnil Delalic, because he could support us financially.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In this videotape, on this occasion did Zejnil Delalic tell the journalist whether he was in charge of carrying out this task -- do you know this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know it and on videotapes you can also tell that he was in charge, that he was ordered by the municipal authorities to complete this task.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sultanic, let us round off this question of the train. After 7 June 1992, did you continue to cooperate with Mr. Zejnil Delalic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. For almost the whole month we had contacts with Mr. Zejnil Delalic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us briefly what those activities consisted of?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Certainly. The first activity was that the electric supply network was out of order in many places and the long distance cables that provided power for our station was also damaged, so it was necessary to bridge this from another long distance cable, so in the event of a fault in this one, this other one could be used, and that there would be no interruption in the regular rail traffic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
